title: Ang 830–831: the ninth Guru in Bilaval
tomorrow: what would a week look like if every day pointed to one name?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Arjan's shelter: sheltered inside a line drawn all the way around, the hot wind outside. Today the ninth Guru asks who really helps.

Someone's grandmother is in the hospital, and the family group chat goes quiet. Everyone loves her. Nobody can fix it. On ang 830, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, sings straight into that kind of silence. His answer has old stories in it, and an elephant.
screen: `THE CHAT GOES QUIET.` → `EVERYONE LOVES HER.` → `NOBODY CAN FIX IT.`

segments.voice: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Bilaval are short, and they circle one question: in trouble, who helps? His answer, in paraphrase: know the Lord's Name as the remover of pain. Remembering it, Ajamal and Ganika were set free. The elephant's terror ended in a moment, as soon as he called on the Lord. These are stories from older Indian tradition: a man who had strayed, a courtesan, an elephant caught in the water. The next hymn presses harder. In paraphrase: without the Lord, no one is your help. Whose mother, father, child or wife? Who is anyone's brother? It sounds cold until you hear it in that quiet group chat. The Guru isn't saying family doesn't love you. He's saying love can't always reach in, and the Name can. Now a neighbor. Jews and Christians both pray the Psalms, and Psalm 46 opens, in the King James words: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." The same question, and the answer points the same way: help in trouble, near, from God. And one honest difference. The psalm speaks as "we," a whole people, and goes on to say they will not fear. The ninth Guru speaks to one mind at a time, and points it to the Name, remembered. Two traditions side by side, neither one needing the other to be wrong.
screen: `THE NAME REMOVES PAIN.` · `AJAMAL, GANIKA, THE ELEPHANT.` · `WHO IS ANYONE'S BROTHER?` · `A NEIGHBOR: A VERY PRESENT HELP.` · then, large: `THE NINTH.`

segments.voice: Count slowly on your fingers the times help came when you couldn't help yourself: a person, a call, a door that opened. Stop at whatever number feels true, and rest with your hand open for the rest of the sit. If you'd like, read the hymns on ang 830 first.
Ang 830. Where Guru Tegh Bahadur's Bilaval hymns begin: the Name as the remover of pain, and the elephant's terror ended.
The ninth: when love can't reach in, the Name still can. Day one hundred of the walk.
